algorithms.title: 0/1 Knapsack
algorithms.reframe: It is not a hunt for the best value per kilogram. It is a longest path through a grid, and an integer program whose linear relaxation sits strictly above it.
algorithms.oneLine: Three items, a ten-kilogram pack, and a table whose bottom-right cell is the answer.
tldr: The state is a cell (i, c): the best value from the first i items inside capacity c. The recurrence is V(i,c) = max(V(i−1,c), vᵢ + V(i−1, c−wᵢ)), and the cell grid is a DAG whose longest path is the optimum.

Value-per-kilogram greedy takes the tent and stops at 42; the optimum takes the stove and the food for 58. Greedy solves the fractional relaxation instead, whose optimum here is 66 — an integrality gap of 8.
The DP is O(nW): polynomial in the capacity's value and exponential in the bits that write it, so the problem is only weakly NP-hard (Karp 1972).
Scaling every value by ε·v_max/n turns the same DP into an O(n²/ε) scheme, fully polynomial because it is polynomial in 1/ε as well as n (Ibarra–Kim 1975, Sahni 1975).

algorithms.title: Bellman–Ford
algorithms.reframe: It is not a slower Dijkstra. It is the least fixed point of a monotone relaxation operator.
algorithms.oneLine: Relax every edge in rounds; stop when nothing improves.
tldr: The state is one distance vector; a round applies the relaxation operator to every edge at once.
The operator is monotone and deflationary, so n−1 rounds reach the fixed point of the Bellman equation.
The n-th round is the negative-cycle test, and a reachable negative cycle is exactly the case where no fixed point exists.
In min-plus algebra the same run reads one row of the tropical closure, the sum of L^(k) for k up to n−1.

algorithms.title: Binary Search
algorithms.reframe: It is not looking at the middle element. It is the halving of an interval of possible answers.
algorithms.oneLine: Halve the interval that still contains the answer, one comparison at a time.
tldr: The state is an interval that always contains the answer; every comparison deletes at least half of what is left.
T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 solves to floor(log2 n) + 1, which is ceil(log2(n+1)) — the logarithm derived, not assumed.
k two-outcome comparisons reach at most 2^k leaves, so n + 1 possible answers force k >= ceil(log2(n+1)): binary search is exactly optimal in the comparison model, and the model is the fine print.
The same boundary search is bisection, because every false-then-true predicate has a first-true position.

algorithms.title: Bipartite Matching
algorithms.reframe: It is not pairing things up greedily. It is a set of independent edges, grown along augmenting paths and pinned from both sides.
algorithms.oneLine: Four applicants, four placements, six acceptable pairs, and a ceiling of three.
tldr: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints; greedy first-available pairing can strand a vertex that an augmenting path would have saved.
Hall's condition (Hall 1935) certifies impossibility from the left: the pair {Cara, Dan} shares a single neighbour, so no matching covers all four applicants.
Berge's condition (Berge 1957) certifies optimality from the search: with no augmenting path left, the size-3 matching is maximum.
König's theorem (König 1931) pins the same number from the cover side, and the unit-capacity flow reduction (Ford–Fulkerson 1956) makes it fall out of pipes.

algorithms.title: Breadth-First Search
algorithms.reframe: It is not a traversal order. It is the distance function of a graph, written one level at a time.
algorithms.oneLine: One source, one queue, and the distance of every vertex — a level at a time.
tldr: The output is a level function: the least fixed point of d(v) = 1 + min d(u) over neighbours — distance in the unweighted metric.
A plain queue is enough because the frontier stays sorted by distance and never spans more than two adjacent levels.
One sweep also decides bipartiteness: colouring by level parity is proper exactly when no edge joins two vertices of equal level (König 1936).

algorithms.title: Coin Change
algorithms.reframe: It is not the largest-coin-first rule. It is a shortest path over the amounts, and greedy is exact exactly when the coin system is canonical.
algorithms.oneLine: The fewest coins that sum to an amount, and the exact condition under which the largest-first rule finds them.
tldr: Every cell of the table is a shortest-path distance on the amounts 0 to the amount, where each coin is an edge of weight one.
Greedy spends 4 + 1 + 1 on 6 with coins 1, 3 and 4; the true minimum is 3 + 3, and the table's corner reads 2.
Greedy is optimal for every amount exactly when the coin system is canonical, a property Pearson 2005 decides in O(n³) even though the largest coin may be huge.
The general minimum-coin problem is only weakly NP-hard: the standard O(n·amount) table is polynomial once the amount is written in unary.

algorithms.title: Depth-First Search
algorithms.reframe: It is not a plunge down one path. It is a spanning forest whose vertices carry nested time intervals.
algorithms.oneLine: Two time-stamps per vertex, and the way the intervals they bound stand to each other.
tldr: Every vertex gets a discovery time and a finish time; the intervals they bound are either nested or disjoint, never partially overlapping (the parenthesis theorem).
A digraph has a cycle exactly when the search produces a back edge — an arc to a vertex still open on the stack.
Reverse the finishing order of a DAG and you have a topological sort; the same times give articulation points and strong components.

algorithms.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
algorithms.reframe: It is not a search for a shortest path. It is a wavefront settling vertices in increasing distance: a one-sided metric closure.
algorithms.oneLine: One source, one frontier, labels that only fall.
tldr: The state is a vector of over-estimates plus a settled set; relaxation only lowers a label.
Greedy is exact because weights are non-negative: once the least label is settled, no later walk can undercut it.
The settled vector is one row of the min-plus closure of the weight matrix — Floyd–Warshall and Lehmann compute the whole closure, Dijkstra computes a row.
One negative edge breaks the exchange step: a later walk undercuts a settled vertex and the run reports a wrong distance.

algorithms.title: Edit Distance
algorithms.reframe: It is not a count of differing characters. It is the geodesic distance in the graph of all strings, where each edit is an edge.
algorithms.oneLine: The fewest insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one string into another.
tldr: Every cell of the table is a shortest-path distance in the graph of strings, and hovering it lights the three edges that reach it.
With insert and delete only, the distance collapses to the identity m + n − 2·LCS.
A test for distance ≤ k needs only the diagonal band |i − j| ≤ k — O(nk) cells, not the O(n²) full table.

algorithms.title: Fixed-Point Iteration
algorithms.reframe: It is not the loop xₙ₊₁ = g(xₙ). It is a contraction of a complete metric space, pulled to its one fixed point at rate qⁿ.
algorithms.oneLine: Repeat x = cos x from any start and watch the cobweb spiral into the Dottie number.
tldr: A map that shrinks every distance by a fixed factor q < 1 has exactly one fixed point, and plain iteration reaches it (Banach 1922).
The error halves geometrically: the panel's ratio column settles on q = 0.6736 for x = cos x, and the chart below plots the honest decay.
The check you actually run is calculus: if |g′(x)| ≤ q < 1 on an interval, the mean value theorem makes g a contraction there.
Newton's method is the special case g′(x*) = 0, which is why its error squares instead of shrinking geometrically.

algorithms.title: Floyd–Warshall
algorithms.reframe: It is not all-pairs shortest paths. It closes one matrix over a semiring, and the arithmetic you choose is the problem you are solving.
algorithms.oneLine: One triple loop, four arithmetics, four different answers from the same grid.
tldr: The four-line triple loop uses only ⊕, ⊗, 0 and 1; the semiring axioms are its entire hypothesis.
Swap the semiring and the same grid reads as cheapest routes, route counts, reachability, or longest routes.
The in-place update is exact when ⊕ is idempotent, so addition — the one non-idempotent choice — is the panel that over-counts.
The closure is a matrix inverse in a semiring: A* = I + A + A² + ⋯ = (I − A)⁻¹ when the series converges.

algorithms.title: Huffman Coding
algorithms.reframe: It is not a compression trick. It is the prefix-code tree of least weighted path length, and its cost is trapped between the entropy H and H + 1.
algorithms.oneLine: Merge the two lightest roots; the accumulated cost is the average code length, and it lands within one bit of the entropy.
tldr: Every merge adds the two merged weights to a running total, so when a single tree remains that total equals the average code length sum of p_i times l_i. The panel accumulates it as you merge and shows it against H.
The two lightest roots are siblings in some optimal tree, by an exchange argument (Huffman 1952). Merge any heavier pair first and the axis prices the mistake in bits.
Shannon 1948 gave the entropy H as the lower bound for any prefix code, and Huffman's rule attains the minimum L*, so entropy is at most L* and L* is less than H + 1.
The one-bit gap is a worst case, not the rule. On the board's six weights H = 2.2037 and L* = 2.25, a gap of 0.05 bits; a two-symbol 0.99/0.01 source has H = 0.0808 against L = 1, a gap of 0.92.

Prefix-free is the whole requirement: no code word is a prefix of another, so the bit string decodes with no delimiters. Symbols sit at the leaves of the tree and that leaf placement is exactly what makes the property hold.

algorithms.title: Karatsuba Multiplication
algorithms.reframe: It is not a faster way to multiply big numbers. It is the rank of polynomial multiplication dropping from four to three.
algorithms.oneLine: One product saved at each split, recursed into the exponent n^log₂3.
tldr: Splitting an n-digit number in half turns four products into three: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + Θ(n), which solves to Θ(n^log₂3) ≈ Θ(n^1.585) against schoolbook's Θ(n²).
The saving is one rank: the two-block product is a rank-4 bilinear map, and Karatsuba is a rank-3 decomposition — the move Strassen makes with two indices instead of one.
The additions cost Θ(n), a lower polynomial degree than the rank's exponent, so they ride along as a constant factor and the rank shows through.
Toom–Cook splits into r parts for 2r − 1 products per node and drops the exponent toward 1; Schönhage–Strassen's FFT reaches O(n log n log log n).
The true complexity of integer multiplication is unknown: the only general lower bound is Ω(n), and the best known upper bound is O(n log n).

algorithms.title: Longest Common Subsequence
algorithms.reframe: It is not the letters two strings share. It is the tallest chain in the product of their prefix orders, and the DP table labels every cell with its height.
algorithms.oneLine: The longest word that appears, in order, inside both strings.
tldr: A common subsequence is a chain in the product order on the matching cells (i, j) with a[i] = b[j]; the DP table writes the height of each rectangle into its corner.
With insert and delete only, the distance between the strings is exactly m + n − 2·LCS — the cost of the cheapest monotone staircase through the grid.
Computing the length is O(mn), but the number of distinct longest common subsequences can be 2^(n/2): polynomial to measure, exponential to list.
When one string is a rearrangement of the other, LCS is exactly the longest increasing subsequence of the position permutation.

algorithms.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
algorithms.reframe: It is not a hunt for a subsequence. It is the tallest chain in a two-dimensional order, and patience sorting builds the antichain cover that matches it.
algorithms.oneLine: The height of the order on the points (i, pᵢ), and the fewest antichains that cover them.
tldr: The state is a partial order on the points (i, pᵢ): comparable means the index and the value both grow. An increasing subsequence is a chain; a non-increasing one is an antichain.

Mirsky 1971: the height equals the fewest antichains that cover the poset. Patience sorting builds that cover, so the pile count is the LIS — and the pile tops stay sorted, so each card costs one binary search.
Dilworth 1950 is the dual, not the same statement: fewest chains equals largest antichain, the width. Credit the pile count to Mirsky, not to Dilworth.
Erdős–Szekeres 1935: more than (r−1)(s−1) numbers force an increasing run of length r or a non-increasing run of length s.

algorithms.title: Maximum Flow
algorithms.reframe: It is not 'push flow until you get stuck'. It is a linear program whose dual is a cut, and the gap between them closes to exactly zero.
algorithms.oneLine: Seven pipes, five junctions, and the cut that certifies the answer.
tldr: The state is a feasible flow, and the maximum flow is the optimum of a linear program whose constraints are one row per junction.
The dual of that program is a cut, so every flow value is at most every cut capacity at every single step — weak duality, visible as a gap card that can never go negative.
Integral capacities give an integral optimum because the network matrix is totally unimodular, so no rounding is ever needed.
Ford–Fulkerson can fail to terminate on irrational capacities (Ford–Fulkerson 1962; Zwick 1995); Edmonds–Karp's shortest-path rule removes the danger at O(VE²).

algorithms.title: Merge Sort
algorithms.reframe: It is not splitting an array and stitching it back. It is the reduction of sorting to merging.
algorithms.oneLine: Every sort is a merge; every merge is one linear pass over two chains.
tldr: Merging sorted lists of lengths p and q costs at most p + q − 1 comparisons, and that join is the only work any level does.
The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) sums to Θ(n log n): each of the log n levels touches every key exactly once.
For n = 2^k the worst case is exactly n log₂ n − n + 1 comparisons — a derived identity, not an estimate.
That matches the floor ⌈log₂(n!)⌉ = Θ(n log n) to a constant factor, so no comparison sort can beat it asymptotically.

algorithms.title: Minimum Spanning Tree
algorithms.reframe: It is not taking the cheapest edges and hoping. It is finding a minimum-weight basis of a matroid, and greedy is exact because the cut and cycle properties are that matroid's exchange axiom.
algorithms.oneLine: One weighted graph, two greedy orders, one forced total — and the axiom that makes greedy provably right.
tldr: A spanning tree is a basis of the graphic matroid; a minimum spanning tree is a minimum-weight basis.
The cut property and the cycle property are the two faces of Whitney's exchange axiom, and each one proves greedy exact.
Ties decide the tree, never the weight: on the graph below there are exactly two minimum spanning trees, one edge-swap apart.
Greedy breaks the instant independence stops being a matroid — three items and one capacity are enough to see it.

algorithms.title: Newton's Method
algorithms.reframe: It is not the update rule xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ). It is the tangent line followed down to the axis, and at a simple root each step squares the error.
algorithms.oneLine: Take the tangent at the current guess, read where it crosses the axis, and watch the correct digits double.
tldr: The step is one tangent line. Replace f by its tangent at (xₙ, f(xₙ)) and set the next guess where that line hits the axis; the panel draws exactly that segment from guess to axis.
A Taylor expansion at a simple root gives eₙ₊₁ = |f″(x*)/2f′(x*)|·eₙ², so the order is 2. At √2 with f(x) = x² − 2 the constant is 1/(2√2) = 0.3536, the number the panel's ratio column settles on.
Newton's map N(x) = x − f(x)/f′(x) is a fixed-point iteration, and N′(x*) = f(x*)f″(x*)/f′(x*)² vanishes at a simple root; the fixed point is superattracting (Fatou 1918, Julia 1918).
Where the tangent is nearly flat the step is enormous: from x₀ = 0.82 on Wallis's cubic x³ − 2x − 5 the first iterate lands near 355, not near the root.
Bisection trades speed for a guarantee. A sign change is enough for a continuous f, and each step at least halves the error, order 1 against Newton's order 2.

algorithms.title: Quicksort
algorithms.reframe: It is not choosing a pivot and partitioning. It is a random binary search tree built by comparison, and the running time is the depth of that tree.
algorithms.oneLine: Every comparison is an edge in a tree; the bill is the tree's depth, summed.
tldr: The pivot sequence is a binary search tree — the one built by inserting the keys in input order — and the comparison count is its internal path length.
Linearity of expectation over the pair indicators gives the exact average E[C] = 2(n+1)H_n − 4n ≈ 1.39 n log₂ n; the constant is 2 ln 2.
A 1:9 split is still Θ(n log n): the depth is log₁₀/₉ n ≈ 6.58 log₂ n, a constant factor, not a new class.
Sorted input with a first-element pivot is a path: n(n−1)/2 ≈ n²/2 comparisons, and McIlroy's 1999 adversary forces that on any deterministic pivot rule.

algorithms.title: Stable Matching
algorithms.reframe: It is not a search over matchings. It is deferred acceptance, and the matching that survives the process is the one no pair wants to leave.
algorithms.oneLine: Propose, hold the best offer, reject the rest: how two preference lists become a stable matching, and why its two ends are the extremes.
tldr: Proposals travel down the proposer's list and each receiver holds the best offer it has seen. Whenever a held offer is replaced, a better proposer has arrived, so the proposer side never withdraws an offer that was accepted.
It stops with no blocking pair: a left–right pair who both rank the other above the partner they were assigned. The board checks every pair and prints that count as zero (Gale–Shapley 1962).

The result is proposer-optimal. Among all stable matchings it is best for every proposer at once and worst for every receiver; swap who proposes and the board recomputes the other extreme (Gale–Shapley 1962, Dubins–Freedman 1981).
The stable matchings of one instance form a lattice (Knuth 1976). The board's four-by-four has exactly two, and the two extremes differ in two of the four assignments.
Termination is counting: each proposer walks down its own list and never repeats a proposal, so the process stops after at most |L|·|R| proposals (McVitie–Wilson 1971).

algorithms.title: Strassen's Algorithm
algorithms.reframe: It is not multiplying matrices in a clever order. It is lowering the rank of a tensor, and the rank sets the exponent.
algorithms.oneLine: Seven products where the textbook needs eight, applied to half-size blocks over and over.
tldr: Matrix multiplication is a bilinear map; the fewest scalar products that compute it is the rank of its tensor, and the textbook algorithm is an 8-term decomposition.
Strassen gave a 7-term one for 2×2 blocks, and Winograd proved seven is the least possible, so that rank is exactly 7 — you cannot do better at size 2.
Recursing gives T(n) = 7T(n/2) + Θ(n²), hence Θ(n^{log₂ 7}) ≈ Θ(n^2.807): the Θ(n²) additions enlarge the constant, not the exponent.
That exponent is ω, the object of a fifty-year race that has moved the bound many times and has never settled it.

algorithms.title: Topological Sort
algorithms.reframe: It is not a linear order of the vertices. It is a linear extension of a partial order.
algorithms.oneLine: Flatten a dependency DAG into a queue order, and see the orders you did not choose.
tldr: Reachability is a preorder; quotient it by mutual reachability and you get the poset you are really sorting.
A topological order is a linear extension — one total order that never contradicts a prerequisite.
Kahn's peeling deletes minimal elements in O(V+E), yet counting how many linear extensions exist is #P-complete (Brightwell–Winkler 1991), so the count is not a construction.

algorithms.title: Union–Find
algorithms.reframe: It is not an algorithm. It is a partition, climbing a lattice.
algorithms.oneLine: Two operations on the partitions of a finite set.
tldr: The state is a partition; union is the join in the partition lattice.
A non-negative potential turns amortised cost into a balance you cannot overdraw.
Rank/size caps height and path compression kills repeats; together the bound is α(n) — smaller than any logarithm you have met.
